common_name: Southern Charm Mullein (Mixed Pastel Peach-Lilac-Cream Verbascum)

planting.note: Sow seeds on the surface of well-drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil (do not cover — seeds need light) in early spring or early fall; Southern Charm is a mixed-color seed strain producing a soft blend of peach, lilac, cream, and rose tones across a planting.

directions: Sow seeds on the soil surface in lean, very well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; good drainage is essential, since mullein rots readily in heavy, wet soil. Southern Charm is a mixed pastel seed strain producing spikes in a soft blend of peach, apricot, lilac, rose, and cream, each flower centered with contrasting purple-mauve stamens, a gentler and more varied palette than the solid yellow of the wild species. It flowers over a long season from late spring into summer and self-seeds modestly to maintain a colony, with seedlings varying somewhat in exact color since it is grown from seed rather than as a single named clone. Deadhead spent spikes to tidy the planting and encourage a longer bloom period, and it combines especially well with Mediterranean herbs, silver-leaved plants, and ornamental grasses in a lean, dry border.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in lean, very well-drained soil in full sun in early spring or early fall; Clementine bears vivid apricot-orange flowers, a warmer tone than most garden mullein hybrids.

directions: Plant in lean, very well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; good drainage matters more than fertility, since rich, wet soil leads to rot and weak growth. Clementine bears dense spikes of vivid apricot-orange flowers, each centered with contrasting purple-mauve stamens, over gray-green, felted foliage that adds textural interest even before bloom. Its warm color makes a striking companion to blue-flowered perennials like salvia or catmint in a sunny border. Deadhead spent spikes to tidy the planting and encourage continued bloom over a long summer season, and expect this hybrid mullein to be relatively short-lived, often performing best as a biennial or short-lived perennial that benefits from occasional replacement or self-sown replacements.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in lean, very well-drained soil in full sun in early spring or early fall; Jackie stays more compact than many mullein hybrids, fitting smaller borders and front-of-border placement.

directions: Plant in lean, very well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; good drainage is essential, since mullein rots readily in heavy, wet soil. Jackie produces compact spikes of soft peachy-pink flowers with contrasting purple-mauve stamens over gray-green, felted foliage, staying notably shorter and more compact than many mullein hybrids, which suits it to smaller borders, rock gardens, and the front of a sunny bed where taller mulleins would be out of scale. Deadhead spent spikes to tidy the planting and encourage continued bloom over a long season from late spring into summer. Like other hybrid mulleins it tends to be relatively short-lived, so allowing some self-seeding or taking root cuttings helps maintain the planting over time.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in lean, very well-drained soil in full sun in early spring or early fall; Helen Johnson bears unusual coppery apricot-rose flowers that shift subtly in tone as they age and as light changes through the day.

directions: Plant in lean, very well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; good drainage matters more than fertility for this rot-prone perennial. Helen Johnson bears dense spikes of unusual coppery apricot-rose flowers, each centered with contrasting purple-mauve stamens, a subtle, shifting color that reads differently depending on the light and time of day, over gray-green, felted foliage. Its distinctive, muted coloring makes it a favorite for designers working with warm, earthy border palettes alongside heucheras, coral bells, and other coppery-toned companions. Deadhead spent spikes to tidy the planting and encourage continued bloom, and expect this hybrid to be relatively short-lived, often performing best as a biennial or short-lived perennial refreshed by occasional self-sown seedlings.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in lean, very well-drained soil in full sun in early spring or early fall; Banana Custard bears soft, creamy-yellow flowers, a gentler tone than the brighter gold of the wild mullein species.

directions: Plant in lean, very well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; good drainage is essential, since this rot-prone perennial declines quickly in heavy, wet soil. Banana Custard produces dense spikes of soft, creamy-yellow flowers with contrasting purple-mauve stamens over gray-green, felted foliage, a gentler, more muted tone than the brighter gold of common wild mullein. Its soft color blends easily into cottage-style plantings alongside pastel companions without dominating the color scheme. Deadhead spent spikes to tidy the planting and encourage continued bloom over a long season from late spring into summer, and expect this hybrid mullein to be relatively short-lived, benefiting from occasional replacement or self-sown seedlings to maintain the planting over the years.
